title: Vine Boom
blurb: The Vine Boom — the deep bass hit that turns any pause into a punchline. Born on Vine, resurrected by meme editors, it's now the internet's default way to underline a moment: someone says something wild, the camera zooms, boom. Use it for dramatic zooms, awkward silences, and revelations that deserve a subwoofer. Arguably the most-used editing sound of the decade, and still not tired.
origin: Originated as a bass drop sound on Vine; became the universal meme emphasis hit.

title: Bruh
blurb: Bruh. The single most efficient expression of disappointment in the English language, in audio form. This is the classic deadpan clip that punctuates fails, bad takes, and moments of profound secondhand embarrassment. It works precisely because it's flat — no drama, just resignation. A foundational sound for any soundboard: when words fail, bruh doesn't.
origin: From a viral basketball reaction clip; became the internet's universal disappointment sound.

title: Goofy Ahh
blurb: The goofy ahh sound — a chaotic cartoon-adjacent noise from the meme genre that turned every serious moment into a circus. Goofy ahh culture is about maximal silliness applied to minimal situations, and this clip is its anthem. Drop it on anyone taking themselves too seriously: workout videos, dramatic speeches, LinkedIn posts. Instant deflation, every time.
origin: From the 'goofy ahh' meme wave — cartoonish sounds applied to overly serious clips.

title: Fart
blurb: The fart sound. Comedy's oldest special effect, undefeated since the invention of air. This is the clean, classic version — the one that works on toddlers, CEOs, and everyone in between, because absolutely nobody is above it. Use it for chair pranks, video punchlines, or the precise moment someone sits down in a quiet meeting. Timeless, shameless, essential.
origin: The eternal classic. No origin needed; farts predate the internet.

title: Loud Fart
blurb: The loud fart — same joke as the regular fart, but with conviction. This one isn't sneaking past anyone: it's a full-volume, room-stopping declaration. Deploy when subtlety has failed, when the moment demands commitment, or when you need to end a conversation immediately and forever. Pairs beautifully with a slow dramatic zoom or the Vine Boom for maximum cinema.
origin: The fart, but louder. Escalation is a valid comedic strategy.

title: Wet Fart
blurb: The wet fart — the high-risk variant. Where the classic fart is innocent comedy, this one carries consequences, and every listener knows it instantly. That extra layer of implied disaster is what makes it the connoisseur's choice for prank content and fail-video punctuation. Use it when a regular fart isn't disrespectful enough for the situation.
origin: The fart taxonomy's most dangerous branch.

title: Emotional Damage
blurb: EMOTIONAL DAMAGE — Steven He's iconic catchphrase, delivered with the energy of a critical hit landing on someone's soul. The internet adopted it as the official sound of a roast connecting: play it right after someone gets destroyed in chat, in a game, or by their own grandmother. One of the most recognizable reaction sounds of the 2020s, still landing daily.
origin: From comedian Steven He's viral videos; the sound of a devastating burn landing.

title: Bad to the Bone Riff
blurb: The opening riff of Bad to the Bone — the sound of someone who thinks they're the main character. Meme culture uses it strictly ironically: the toddler in sunglasses, the cat knocking a glass off the table, anyone doing something mildly rebellious with maximum swagger. Play it when someone breaks the smallest possible rule and looks proud about it.
origin: George Thorogood's 1982 riff, repurposed by memes as ironic badass entrance music.

title: Sad Violin
blurb: The sad violin — the melodramatic string melody that plays when something mildly unfortunate gets treated like a Shakespearean tragedy. The meme version, specifically: it's for dropped ice cream cones, missed buses, and gamers dying to the easiest enemy. Maximum pathos applied to minimum stakes. A cornerstone of ironic editing since the YouTube montage era.
origin: The classic ironic-tragedy backing track from the YouTube montage era.

title: Why Are You Running?
blurb: WHY ARE YOU RUNNING? — the legendary line from a Nigerian film scene that became one of the internet's favorite chase-scene audios. The delivery is everything: genuine bewilderment escalating into full pursuit. Use it over any video of something fleeing — pets, toddlers, roombas, your motivation on Monday morning. A certified hall-of-famer.
origin: From a Nollywood film scene that went globally viral around 2018.

title: Yeet
blurb: YEET — the battle cry of throwing something with zero regard for where it lands. What started as a dance and a vine became the internet's official projectile-launching sound. Play it the moment anything becomes airborne: a water bottle, a controller after a loss, your responsibilities on Friday afternoon. Short, loud, and perfectly stupid.
origin: From a 2014 Vine; became the universal sound of throwing things enthusiastically.

title: Huh? (Cat)
blurb: The Huh? cat sound — a bewildered little noise that perfectly captures the moment comprehension fails. Attached to the famous confused-cat meme, it's the audio equivalent of a head tilt. Use it when someone says something that makes no sense, when instructions are unclear, or when you check your bank account. Small sound, enormous relatability.
origin: Paired with the viral confused cat meme; the sound of pure bafflement.

title: Baby Laughing
blurb: The baby laughing meme sound — an unstoppable cascade of infant giggles that is scientifically impossible not to smile at. Editors use it two ways: sincerely, over genuinely wholesome content, and diabolically, over someone's misfortune, where the innocence makes it ten times more brutal. Both uses are correct. One of the most versatile laugh tracks on the internet.
origin: A viral baby-laughter clip adopted as both a wholesome and a savage reaction sound.

title: Metal Pipe Falling
blurb: The metal pipe falling sound — an absurdly loud CLANG that became one of the defining meme sounds of the 2020s. It's the designated audio for sudden catastrophic failure: someone slips, a plan collapses, a sentence goes somewhere it shouldn't. The comedy is in the excessive volume applied to minor events. Warning: genuinely loud. That's the point.
origin: A stock metal-impact recording that meme editors turned into the sound of disaster.

title: Wilhelm Scream
blurb: The Wilhelm Scream — cinema's most famous inside joke. This stock scream has appeared in over 400 films since 1951, from Star Wars to Indiana Jones, snuck in by sound designers as a tradition. Once you know it, you hear it everywhere. Use it for falls, explosions, and any moment that deserves a distinctly theatrical demise. A genuine piece of film history in button form.
origin: Recorded in 1951 for 'Distant Drums'; named after a character shot by an arrow in a 1953 western.

title: Windows XP Error
blurb: The Windows XP error ding — the sound of something going wrong in 2003, permanently burned into the memory of everyone who grew up with a family computer. Today it's pure nostalgic comedy: play it when someone makes a mistake and watch a generation flinch. Works in edits as a fail sound with vintage flavor. The most famous error chime ever shipped.
origin: The critical-error chime from Microsoft Windows XP (2001).

title: Law & Order Dun Dun
blurb: DUN DUN. The Law & Order scene-transition sound — two notes that instantly mean a crime has been committed and justice is being pursued. The internet uses it as a gavel: play it after any accusation, verdict, or petty judgment in the group chat. It turns 'you ate my leftovers' into a felony proceeding. Iconic, authoritative, endlessly funny out of context.
origin: The scene-change sting from Law & Order, created by composer Mike Post.

title: Record Scratch
blurb: The record scratch — the sound that stops time. Paired forever with a freeze-frame and 'yep, that's me — you're probably wondering how I got here,' it's the universal signal that something has gone off script. Use it to interrupt, to rewind, or to open any story that starts at the worst possible moment. A cornerstone of comedic editing grammar.
origin: The vinyl-scratch interrupt, canonized by the freeze-frame narration trope.

title: Dun Dun Dunnn!
blurb: Dun dun DUNNN — the melodramatic orchestral sting that announces a shocking revelation, whether or not the revelation is actually shocking. That's the joke: play it when someone reveals they forgot to buy milk. The bigger the gap between the drama of the sound and the triviality of the moment, the harder it lands. Essential punctuation for fake-serious storytelling.
origin: The classic melodrama sting, parodied since radio-drama days.

title: Cash Register (Cha-Ching)
blurb: Cha-ching — the mechanical cash register bell that means money has changed hands. The internet's sound for profit in every form: a good deal, a paycheck hitting, a scheme coming together. Streamers fire it on donations; editors use it when anyone so much as mentions money. Satisfying, greedy, and universally understood in any language.
origin: The classic mechanical register bell, meme shorthand for profit.

title: Apple Pay
blurb: The Apple Pay success chime — that soft, expensive-sounding ding of a payment going through. The meme usage is beautifully unhinged: it plays whenever anything is 'purchased,' including things that cannot be purchased — dignity, someone's ankles in a basketball game, a person getting dunked on in an argument. One of the most searched notification sounds on the internet.
origin: Apple's contactless-payment confirmation chime, memed as the sound of 'buying' anything.

title: iPhone Notification
blurb: The iPhone notification sound — arguably the most heard sound on Earth. Every human within earshot will check their phone; that reflex is undefeated and always will be. Use it in edits to signal an incoming text, or play it in a quiet room as a social experiment with immediate and total results. The apex predator of prank sounds.
origin: Apple's default alert tone; the most reflexively recognized sound in modern life.

title: Taco Bell Bong
blurb: The Taco Bell bong — the resonant bell that ends every Taco Bell ad and, somehow, became a beloved meme sound. Editors drop it after anything that could conceivably end a commercial: a punchline, a life decision, a catastrophic failure presented with confidence. It carries an odd finality, like the universe signing off on whatever just happened.
origin: The gong sting from Taco Bell's commercials; adopted as an all-purpose closing punctuation.

title: Among Us Role Reveal
blurb: The Among Us role reveal sound — the ominous shimmer that told you whether you were crewmate or impostor. During 2020 it played in ten million bedrooms a night; now it's the meme sound for any secret identity being revealed. Use it when someone's true nature comes out: the friend who was the group chat leaker all along, revealed at last.
origin: From Among Us's game-start role assignment screen (InnerSloth, 2018).

title: Among Us (Sus)
blurb: The Among Us sound of pure suspicion. When something is sus, this is what sus sounds like. The game's audio became inseparable from the concept of suspicion itself — a linguistic takeover no one saw coming. Play it when someone's story doesn't add up, when the vent opens, or when anyone behaves even slightly unusually near a task.
origin: From Among Us, the game that made 'sus' a permanent part of the language.

title: Mario Coin
blurb: The Mario coin sound — the brightest, most satisfying blip in gaming history. Forty years of players are neurologically conditioned to feel rewarded by this exact noise, which makes it comedy gold when applied to worthless achievements: finding a penny, getting a participation trophy, receiving exposure instead of payment. The gold standard of reward sounds, literally.
origin: The coin collect from Super Mario Bros. (Nintendo, 1985).

title: FNAF Jumpscare Scream
blurb: The Five Nights at Freddy's jumpscare scream — the shriek that launched a thousand reaction videos. This is the sound of an animatronic deciding your shift is over. A decade later it still triggers fight-or-flight in anyone who played FNAF at a formative age. Use it for jump scares, fake-outs, and pranking friends with headphones. Volume warning very much intended.
origin: The animatronic jumpscare scream from Five Nights at Freddy's (2014).

title: Hog Rider
blurb: HOG RIDAAAA — the war cry of Clash of Clans' most committed unit, screamed with the confidence of a man riding a hog into certain doom. It became the sound of charging into any situation without a plan: group projects, Black Friday sales, replying-all to a company email. Absolute commitment, zero strategy. An all-time gaming meme sound.
origin: The Hog Rider deployment yell from Clash of Clans / Clash Royale (Supercell).

title: Minecraft Villager
blurb: The Minecraft villager 'hmm' — the confused grunt of gaming's most economically ruthless NPC. It's become the internet's sound for incomprehension and dubious deals alike: play it when someone offers you a terrible trade, when instructions make no sense, or as the response to any question you don't want to answer. Weirdly expressive for a single syllable.
origin: The villager trade grunt from Minecraft (Mojang).

title: Roblox Oof
blurb: The Roblox oof — the tiny death sound that became a generation's word for misfortune. Every Roblox death for over a decade played this exact clip, hardwiring it into millions of childhoods before it was retired from the game — which only made the meme stronger. Play it for any minor disaster: stubbed toes, failed tests, seeing the group project grade.
origin: Roblox's original death sound (2006–2022), retired from the game but immortal as a meme.

title: GTA V Wasted
blurb: WASTED — the Grand Theft Auto death sting, complete with that instantly recognizable thud of failure. The meme format writes itself: apply to any real-world faceplant, rejection, or moment of defeat, ideally with the grayscale filter implied. It's the most cinematic way to announce that someone just got absolutely folded by life. A fail-compilation essential.
origin: The death/arrest sting from Grand Theft Auto V (Rockstar, 2013).

title: Get Out (Tuco)
blurb: GET OUT — Tuco Salamanca's unhinged scream from Breaking Bad, extracted by TikTok and turned into the definitive ejection sound. It plays when anyone or anything needs to leave immediately: bad takes, intrusive thoughts, the wrong answer in a quiz. The delivery is so violently final that it works on literally any subject. One of the most searched meme sounds right now.
origin: Tuco Salamanca's scream from Breaking Bad, viral on TikTok as the universal ejection sound.

title: Skibidi Toilet
blurb: The Skibidi Toilet sound — the anthem of the animated series that conquered Gen Alpha and baffled everyone older. Whatever your stance on brainrot, the numbers don't lie: this audio defined an era of internet culture. Play it to summon children, alarm adults, or acknowledge that the skibidi wars changed us all. A historical document of the 2020s internet.
origin: From DaFuq!?Boom!'s Skibidi Toilet series, the defining Gen Alpha meme franchise.

title: Rizz Sound Effect
blurb: The rizz sound effect — the audio that certifies a successful display of charisma. When someone delivers a line so smooth it shouldn't have worked, this sound makes it official. TikTok plays it over successful flirting, confident walk-ups, and negotiations that end in a phone number. Also devastating when used ironically over a catastrophic attempt. Both modes essential.
origin: TikTok's certification sound for displays of rizz (charisma), ironic or sincere.

title: AUGHHH
blurb: AUGHHH — the guttural scream of a man experiencing everything at once. This TikTok staple is the sound of pure overwhelmed anguish, deployed when words are insufficient: seeing the exam question, checking the price, remembering something embarrassing from 2014 at 3am. It's cathartic, it's dramatic, and it's exactly the noise your soul makes internally.
origin: A viral scream clip adopted by TikTok as the sound of total internal collapse.

title: Oh No No No
blurb: The 'Oh No No No' laugh — the wheezing, escalating laughter that TikTok attaches to disasters in progress. It plays as the skateboard leaves the rail, as the cake begins to lean, as the plan visibly falls apart in real time. The laugh arriving before the impact is the entire art form. A fail-video institution.
origin: The viral laughing track played over slow-motion disasters on TikTok.

title: We Do Not Care
blurb: WE DO NOT CARE — the viral declaration of collective indifference, delivered with a conviction that ends the discussion permanently. TikTok made it the official response to unsolicited opinions, minor drama, and explanations nobody requested. It's not rude, exactly — it's administrative. The matter has been reviewed, and we do not care. Case closed.
origin: A viral TikTok audio adopted as the official dismissal of unwanted information.

title: To Be Continued (JoJo)
blurb: The JoJo's Bizarre Adventure 'To Be Continued' sting — Roundabout's bassline sliding in as time freezes at the worst possible moment. The meme cuts to the arrow-and-text card right as disaster becomes inevitable: the slip has begun, the glass is mid-fall, the sentence cannot be unsaid. One of the greatest editing memes ever devised, and the bass still slaps.
origin: From JoJo's Bizarre Adventure's episode-ending freeze frames, set to Yes's 'Roundabout'.

title: Instant Transmission
blurb: The Instant Transmission sound from Dragon Ball Z — Goku's two-finger teleport, in audio form. The meme uses it for any sudden departure: leaving the party without saying goodbye, exiting a conversation that turned weird, vanishing when the check arrives. That zip means someone is simply no longer there, and no further explanation will be provided.
origin: Goku's teleportation technique sound from Dragon Ball Z.

title: Anime Wow
blurb: The anime 'wow' — a breathless, sparkly-eyed gasp of amazement that anime characters deploy at everything from sunsets to sandwiches. The meme usage is gloriously ironic: play it over the most mundane accomplishment imaginable. Someone parallel parks adequately? Anime wow. The vending machine gives correct change? Anime wow. Cheap awe, infinitely renewable.
origin: The classic wide-eyed anime gasp, memed as ironic amazement at nothing.

title: A Few Moments Later
blurb: 'A few moments later…' — the SpongeBob French narrator time card, the most famous transition in television history. It's the universal signal that time has passed and the situation has somehow gotten worse. Use it between any plan and its consequences: the confident before, the catastrophic after. No editing toolkit is complete without it.
origin: The French narrator time card from SpongeBob SquarePants.

title: Boowomp
blurb: The boowomp — SpongeBob's two-note sad sting, the sound of hopes deflating in real time. It's the perfect small failure sound: not a catastrophe, just a quiet 'oh.' The meme community adopted it for anticlimaxes, rejections delivered politely, and moments where enthusiasm meets reality. Somehow funnier the smaller the disappointment it accompanies.
origin: The classic deflated sting from SpongeBob SquarePants, adopted for gentle failures.

title: SpongeBob Fog Horn
blurb: The SpongeBob fog horn — the blaring ship horn that opens Bikini Bottom's mornings and, for a generation, every episode of their childhood. As a meme it's an alarm clock, an air-raid siren of nostalgia, and a way to announce your presence with unnecessary force. Play it at full volume to start the day like Mr. Krabs smelling money.
origin: The nautical fog horn from SpongeBob SquarePants' iconic openings.

title: SpongeBob Sad Song
blurb: The SpongeBob sad song — that mournful little melody the show plays when things get genuinely melancholy under the sea. The internet uses it with surgical irony: it swells over the smallest inconveniences, turning a dropped fry into a tragedy worthy of a montage. Equal parts nostalgia and comedy, and one of the most requested SpongeBob audios anywhere.
origin: The melancholy interlude music from SpongeBob SquarePants.

title: FBI Open Up
blurb: FBI OPEN UP — the door-splintering announcement followed by implied chaos. The meme plays it whenever someone types, says, or searches something questionable: the joke is that the feds were already outside. As a prank sound it's elite — few audio clips make people physically look at their own front door. Use with a subwoofer for federal-grade impact.
origin: The meme raid announcement, popularized by gaming and Discord culture.

title: Dog Whistle
blurb: The dog whistle sound — high-frequency content that dogs hear clearly and humans mostly don't. Play it and watch every dog in range snap to attention while the humans look around confused. It's a prank on two species simultaneously. Also weirdly useful for testing speakers and headphones at the top of their range. Your dog is about to be very interested in your phone.
origin: A high-frequency whistle tone at the edge of human hearing — dogs hear it fine.
